title: The Listening Walk: Parent Guide
endLine: Our ears are funnels that catch sound.

scenes.tts: How many sounds are there in a quiet backyard? Most of the time we hear without really listening. Two still minutes and a sheet of paper let your child find out.
scenes.caption: How many sounds are there in a quiet backyard? Most of the time we hear without really listening. Two still minutes and a sheet of paper let your child find out.
scenes.visual: Warm schematic backyard seen from a low angle: a lawn, one tree, a fence, a far road edge. Soft wavy sound lines drift in from several directions: from a bird on a branch, from the tree's leaves, from a far car, from a small dog beyond the fence. Large high-contrast text: 'How many sounds?' No photos of real children.
scenes.narration: How many sounds are there in a quiet backyard? Most of the time we hear without really listening. Two still minutes and a sheet of paper let your child find out.

scenes.visual: Same backyard. The title 'The Listening Walk' appears in the sky area while the sound lines keep drifting gently.

scenes.tts: In about thirty minutes, your child sits still, counts sounds, and draws a map of them. Then they test their own ears. Your child practices listening closely, sorting what they hear, and checking a guess.
scenes.caption: In about thirty minutes, your child sits still, counts sounds, and draws a map of them. Then they test their own ears. Your child practices listening closely, sorting what they hear, and checking a guess.
scenes.visual: Same backyard. A towel on the grass, with a clipboard and crayons beside it, slides into the foreground. Three short labels appear one by one: 'Listen closely', 'Sort sounds', 'Guess, then check'. A small clock icon reads '30 minutes'.
scenes.narration: In about thirty minutes, your child sits still, counts sounds, and draws a map of them. Then they test their own ears. Your child practices listening closely, sorting what they hear, and checking a guess.

scenes.tts: Gather paper, crayons, a clipboard or book, a timer, and a mat. Pick a spot you have permission to use, away from roads, driveways, ponds, and streams. Stay close enough to touch.
scenes.caption: Gather paper, crayons, a clipboard or book, a timer, and a mat. Pick a spot you have permission to use, away from roads, driveways, ponds, and streams. Stay close enough to touch.
scenes.visual: Friendly drawn objects settle on the towel: paper, crayons, a clipboard, a phone showing a timer. A soft map-like overlay marks the backyard spot with a check, and a far road and a small pond are faded with a gentle X.
scenes.narration: Gather paper, crayons, a clipboard or book, a timer, and a mat. Pick a spot you have permission to use, away from roads, driveways, ponds, and streams. Stay close enough to touch.

scenes.tts: Ask first, 'How many different sounds do you think we will hear in two minutes?' Write the number down. Then set the timer. Your child closes their eyes and holds up one finger for each new sound.
scenes.caption: Ask first, 'How many different sounds do you think we will hear in two minutes?' Write the number down. Then set the timer. Your child closes their eyes and holds up one finger for each new sound.
scenes.visual: A simple drawn adult and child silhouette sit on the towel, seen from behind. A speech bubble: 'How many sounds?' A small notepad shows a written guess. Then a timer ring starts filling, and the child's raised hand adds one finger each time a new sound line arrives: bird, leaves, car.
scenes.narration: Ask first, 'How many different sounds do you think we will hear in two minutes?' Write the number down. Then set the timer. Your child closes their eyes and holds up one finger for each new sound.

scenes.tts: When the timer ends, ask, 'Was it more or fewer than you thought?' Expect anything from a few sounds to a dozen or more, depending on the place and time of day.
scenes.caption: When the timer ends, ask, 'Was it more or fewer than you thought?' Expect anything from a few sounds to a dozen or more, depending on the place and time of day.
scenes.visual: The timer ring completes. The notepad slides back with the guess next to a tally of finger counts. A speech bubble: 'More or fewer?' The sound lines in the backyard pause and glow once each.
scenes.narration: When the timer ends, ask, 'Was it more or fewer than you thought?' Expect anything from a few sounds to a dozen or more, depending on the place and time of day.

scenes.tts: Now the sound map. Put a dot in the middle of the paper and label it 'me'. Your child draws each sound in the direction it came from. Near sounds go close to the dot, far sounds near the edge.
scenes.caption: Now the sound map. Put a dot in the middle of the paper and label it 'me'. Your child draws each sound in the direction it came from. Near sounds go close to the dot, far sounds near the edge.
scenes.visual: The clipboard paper fills most of the frame. A dot appears in the center labelled 'me'. A small bird drawing appears close to the dot, upper left; a car appears near the right edge, matching where each sound came from in the backyard. Short labels: 'Near: close to dot', 'Far: near edge'.
scenes.narration: Now the sound map. Put a dot in the middle of the paper and label it 'me'. Your child draws each sound in the direction it came from. Near sounds go close to the dot, far sounds near the edge.

scenes.tts: Add one rule at a time. Loud sounds are drawn big, and soft sounds small. High and low are a different thing, called pitch. Add an arrow up for a high sound, and down for a low one.
scenes.caption: Add one rule at a time. Loud sounds are drawn big, and soft sounds small. High and low are a different thing, called pitch. Add an arrow up for a high sound, and down for a low one.
scenes.visual: On the same map, the car drawing grows bigger and a far dog shrinks small. Label: 'Loud: big, soft: small'. Then a small up-arrow appears beside the bird and a down-arrow beside the car. Label: 'High: up, low: down'.
scenes.narration: Add one rule at a time. Loud sounds are drawn big, and soft sounds small. High and low are a different thing, called pitch. Add an arrow up for a high sound, and down for a low one.

scenes.tts: Last, circle the sounds made by living things, like birds, insects, dogs, and people. Talk about the tricky ones. Rustling leaves come from a tree, but the wind makes them move.
scenes.caption: Last, circle the sounds made by living things, like birds, insects, dogs, and people. Talk about the tricky ones. Rustling leaves come from a tree, but the wind makes them move.
scenes.visual: Gold circles appear around the bird, the dog and a small insect on the map. The tree drawing with wind lines gets a dotted circle and a small question mark. Label: 'Tricky: tree or wind?'
scenes.narration: Last, circle the sounds made by living things, like birds, insects, dogs, and people. Talk about the tricky ones. Rustling leaves come from a tree, but the wind makes them move.

scenes.tts: Choose a quiet, steady sound. Use a guarded fan on a stable surface with its cord tucked away. Sit your child at least an arm's length back. Have them face the sound and listen. Then have them cup their hands, fingers together.
scenes.caption: Choose a quiet, steady sound. Use a guarded fan on a stable surface with its cord tucked away. Sit your child at least an arm's length back. Have them face the sound and listen. Then have them cup their hands, fingers together.
scenes.visual: Show the adult setting a guarded fan on a stable, level surface and securing the cord away from the walkway. The adult sits beside the child, who is at least an arm's length from the fan. The child listens while facing the fan, then cups both hands behind their ears with fingers together.
scenes.narration: Choose a quiet, steady sound. Use a guarded fan on a stable surface with its cord tucked away. Sit your child at least an arm's length back. Have them face the sound and listen. Then have them cup their hands, fingers together.

scenes.tts: A question for you. Your child keeps the hands cupped, then turns their back to the fan. Will the sound get louder, fainter, or stay the same?
scenes.caption: A question for you. Your child keeps the hands cupped, then turns their back to the fan. Will the sound get louder, fainter, or stay the same?
scenes.visual: Hold the side view just before the turn. The question card shows three options: 'Louder, fainter, or the same?'
scenes.narration: A question for you. Your child keeps the hands cupped, then turns their back to the fan. Will the sound get louder, fainter, or stay the same?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card. The fan blades turn slowly and the sound lines keep drifting, without revealing the answer.

scenes.tts: Most children hear it louder with hands cupped. Have them turn around with their hands still cupped. It usually sounds fainter. The bigger funnels now face away from the sound.
scenes.caption: Most children hear it louder with hands cupped. Have them turn around with their hands still cupped. It usually sounds fainter. The bigger funnels now face away from the sound.
scenes.visual: The child turns their back to the fan with hands still cupped. Keep the sound from the fan steady. In a side-view inset, show fewer sound lines entering the ears after the turn. Label the demonstration “Usually fainter”.
scenes.narration: Most children hear it louder with hands cupped. Have them turn around with their hands still cupped. It usually sounds fainter. The bigger funnels now face away from the sound.

scenes.tts: Cats and horses have large ears they can turn toward a sound. Ask, 'What do you think a cat's big ears help it do?' Watch only a pet your child knows, and stay beside them.
scenes.caption: Cats and horses have large ears they can turn toward a sound. Ask, 'What do you think a cat's big ears help it do?' Watch only a pet your child knows, and stay beside them.
scenes.visual: A drawn parent and child watch a familiar cat from a little distance as a cupboard opens quietly. The cat swivels its ears. A small inset shows the parent and child outside a horse's fence while an adult who knows the horse handles it on the inside. Speech bubble: 'What do big ears help it do?'
scenes.narration: Cats and horses have large ears they can turn toward a sound. Ask, 'What do you think a cat's big ears help it do?' Watch only a pet your child knows, and stay beside them.

scenes.tts: Stay close enough to touch the whole time. Cup hands only for quiet, everyday sounds, never toward a road. If something loud starts, move away. Nothing goes into the ear.
scenes.caption: Stay close enough to touch the whole time. Cup hands only for quiet, everyday sounds, never toward a road. If something loud starts, move away. Nothing goes into the ear.
scenes.visual: Back to the backyard. Up to four clear safety badges appear: adult and child side by side ('Close enough to touch'), a crossed-out road edge ('Never toward a road'), a mower with an arrow pointing away ('Loud? Move away'), and an ear with a crossed-out cotton swab ('Nothing in ears').
scenes.narration: Stay close enough to touch the whole time. Cup hands only for quiet, everyday sounds, never toward a road. If something loud starts, move away. Nothing goes into the ear.

scenes.tts: Nothing from the ground goes in mouths. Small objects like pebbles and acorns can choke children under four. Call nine one one if a child is choking. Never taste wild plants, berries, or mushrooms. Wash hands after touching them. Check for ticks after sitting in grass.
scenes.caption: Nothing from the ground goes in mouths. Small objects like pebbles and acorns can choke children under four. Call nine one one if a child is choking. Never taste wild plants, berries, or mushrooms. Wash hands after touching them. Check for ticks after sitting in grass.
scenes.visual: Show a crossed-out pebble and acorn labeled 'Under 4: choking risk', then a phone labeled 'Choking: call 911'. Show a crossed-out hand bringing a berry to a mouth. Then show hands washing with soap and water and a parent checking a child's pant leg for ticks.
scenes.narration: Nothing from the ground goes in mouths. Small objects like pebbles and acorns can choke children under four. Call nine one one if a child is choking. Never taste wild plants, berries, or mushrooms. Wash hands after touching them. Check for ticks after sitting in grass.

scenes.tts: Ask what your child noticed when they cupped their hands. Look back at the map together and trace where the sounds came from.
scenes.caption: Ask what your child noticed when they cupped their hands. Look back at the map together and trace where the sounds came from.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full backyard with the towel and the finished sound map lying on it, circles and arrows in place. Soft sound lines drift in again from the bird, the tree and the far road toward the empty towel.
scenes.narration: Ask what your child noticed when they cupped their hands. Look back at the map together and trace where the sounds came from.

scenes.line: Our ears are funnels that catch sound.
scenes.visual: Clean warm end card with a faint sound map in the background. Centered, large, high-contrast text: 'Our ears are funnels that catch sound.'
